top.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
top.detail: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets. / GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities | OpenAI OpenAI November 24, 2026 Science Publication GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities Read the paper (opens in a new window) Share Key findings: Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequence…

top.title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
top.detail: go/codegolf benchmark: frontier models vs. Google's 2015 code golfers. / go/codegolf benchmark go/codegolf benchmark: frontier models vs. Google's 2015 code golfers. 32 problems · 8 languages · 256 cells Loading… Problems Loading… About TL;DR: I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works. Where the problems come from: go/codegolf In 2015, when I was at Google, I spent a lot of time on an internal site called go/codegolf . There was one problem a week, and we competed to write the shortest program that solved it. Most of the regulars were code-golf enthusiasts. Each problem went through three phases: Phase What happens 1. Candidate Any Googler could propose a problem by posting a statement and a full test suite. Everyone could read the tests and suggest fixes. Votes were called LGTMs ; the candidate with the most LGTMs became the next week's problem. 2. Competition (7 days) You could see your own submissions, but nobody else's. Only your shortest passing solution in each language counted. The per-language scoreboards showed sizes, not code.
